screens.title: Design Patterns and MLOps: Bringing ML into Production
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will orient around the practical work of integrating machine learning into real production systems. You will learn why ML changes architecture decisions, which deployment patterns solve different latency and coupling needs, and how MLOps practices keep models healthy over time. Think of an ML model not as a single binary but as a living element: it depends on data pipelines, feature consistency, a model registry, deployment endpoints, and monitoring. For example, an online recommendation call must guarantee low latency and consistent feature values, while a batch scoring job can trade latency for throughput. A common misconception is treating a model like static code. Instead, plan for retraining, versioning, and drift detection from day one. By the end of this chapter you will be able to map a business need — like fraud detection or personalized recommendations — to a concrete pattern, choose serving and monitoring strategies, and sketch an MLOps pipeline that supports continuous delivery. Consider a weekly retraining schedule for a recommendation engine: the pipeline must ingest new events, update features, validate a new model, and then promote it to production safely. What would you monitor first in that flow?

screens.narratorSegment: In this segment we'll set clear goals for what you'll be able to do after working through the lesson. First, you will identify core challenges when integrating ML into existing software, such as the need for continuous data pipelines and the probabilistic nature of models. Second, you'll recognize the main deployment patterns—online, batch, embedded, and remote—and be able to choose the right one based on latency, throughput, and coupling constraints. Third, you'll explain MLOps practices that bring automation, reproducibility, and monitoring to the model lifecycle, including model registries and CI/CD for ML artifacts. Finally, you'll evaluate data infrastructure components like feature stores and data versioning systems so models get consistent inputs in training and production. Each objective includes a short competency measure: sketch a pipeline, pick a serving pattern for a scenario, and propose monitoring and retraining triggers. These skills matter because ML systems require both architectural choices and operational discipline to avoid silent failures or performance decay in production.

screens.title: Why ML changes software architecture
screens.narratorSegment: Machine learning components differ from traditional software in important ways. First, models are probabilistic: they produce predictions based on learned patterns and therefore have uncertainty. That means behavior can change when input data shifts, so you must plan for continuous evaluation. Second, models depend on data pipelines and feature computation; inconsistent feature values between training and serving cause prediction errors known as training/serving skew. Third, the development lifecycle is iterative and multi-disciplinary: data scientists experiment, ML engineers operationalize, and software engineers integrate the service. Architecturally this leads to distinct responsibilities—feature stores to centralize feature computation, model registries to manage artifacts, and deployment services to isolate inference. A concrete example is a product recommender: it needs live user features for online inference and a retraining loop to refresh weights weekly. A common misconception is to treat a model like any library you can version and forget; instead, treat it as a product that requires monitoring, governance, and scheduled updates. Takeaway: plan pipelines, enforce feature consistency, and make retraining part of the architecture. What aspect of your current application would change if a model’s predictions could drift over time?

screens.title: Deployment patterns: online, batch, embedded, remote
screens.narratorSegment: Selecting a deployment pattern is a core architectural decision. Online inference provides low-latency predictions by exposing a model via a real-time endpoint; it is suitable for fraud detection or personalized recommendations where each request needs a decision in milliseconds. Batch inference processes large datasets at scheduled intervals and favors throughput over per-request latency, for example producing daily churn scores for marketing. Embedded models are included directly in application binaries or mobile apps; they reduce network overhead and latency but increase deployment coupling and complicate updates. Remote models are isolated in dedicated prediction services; they offer better scalability and independent lifecycle management but introduce network latency. As a concrete scenario, consider fraud scoring during checkout: online inference is typically preferred because decisions must be immediate. A common misconception is to default to embedded models for speed; however, embedded models can become stale and make rolling updates cumbersome. When choosing a pattern, weigh latency requirements, update cadence, operational complexity, and security boundaries. Which pattern would you choose if your top priority is independent scaling and version control? Deployment patterns: online, batch, embedded, remote means match pattern to requirements: online for low latency, batch for throughput, embedded for tight latency but high coupling, remote for isolation and independent scaling.. In practical terms, trade-offs across latency, coupling, and scalability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison Deployment patterns
Online inference
Low-latency endpoint for single-request predictions. Use for fraud detection or personalization.
Pros
Low latency, independent scaling, model versioning at endpoint level.
Cons
Requires serving infra and runtime monitoring.
Batch inference
Scheduled scoring of large datasets when latency is not critical.
Pros
High throughput, efficient resource utilization.
Cons
Not suitable for real-time decisions.
Embedded models
Model code packaged into the application for minimal network overhead.
Pros
Very low latency, offline capability.
Cons
Harder to update and maintain; increases coupling.
Remote models
Predictions served by an isolated service, often via REST API or gRPC.
Pros
Isolation, independent lifecycle and scaling.
Cons
Adds network latency and operational overhead.
Scenario walk-through
Fraud detection at checkout requires decisions in milliseconds — online inference via a dedicated prediction API is the typical choice because it balances latency and operational controls.
Misconception check
Choosing embedded models solely for speed ignores deployment complexity and update constraints; evaluate lifecycle impacts first.
Key Takeaway

Match serving patterns to business requirements: latency, update cadence, and operational isolation determine the right choice.

screens.title: MLOps fundamentals: versioning, CI/CD, and registries
screens.narratorSegment: MLOps is the operational practice that stitches together experimentation and production delivery for ML models. At its core are automation, reproducibility, and testable deployments. Start with versioning: track code, configuration, data, and model artifacts so you can reproduce results and audit changes. Model registries store artifacts, metadata, and stage transitions — for example staging to production — enabling safe promotion and rollback. CI/CD pipelines for ML should validate not only code but also data integrity and model quality gates; automated tests can include unit tests, data schema checks, and model evaluation against a holdout set. A concrete example is a pipeline that runs on new data: first it validates data schemas, then trains a candidate model, logs metrics to a tracking system, compares performance with production, and if it passes quality gates, registers and deploys the model. A common mistake is to rely on manual promotion; automation reduces human error and ensures repeatability. Takeaway: make reproducibility and automated quality checks the backbone of your ML delivery. How would you implement a safety gate that prevents a worse model from being deployed?

Process Flow MLOps fundamentals
Versioning, CI/CD, and model registries
Extend DevOps to model artifacts and data with automated gates and reproducible runs.
1. Data Versioning
Track datasets so training can be reproduced and audited.
2. Training & Validation
Automated runs that log metrics to compare candidates.
3. Model Registry
Store artifacts, metadata, and stages for safe promotion.
4. CI/CD Gates
Automated quality gates: tests, metrics comparison, and canary releases.
Concrete example
A pipeline validates input schema, trains a candidate model, logs metrics, and only registers the model if it improves upon production according to defined metrics.
Misconception

Key Takeaway

Automate testing and promotion of models and their data so production changes are reproducible and safe.

screens.title: Automated ML pipelines and orchestration
screens.narratorSegment: An automated ML pipeline strings together the stages that move raw events to a deployed model and returning value. The pipeline typically starts with data ingestion and validation: verify schemas and completeness so downstream models are not fed corrupt inputs. Next, compute and materialize features, often in a feature store that can serve both training and online requests. Then execute training and hyperparameter tuning, followed by validation against holdout datasets and business-specific quality gates. If the candidate passes gates, register the model and trigger a deployment step—this may be a canary rollout or a full promotion to production. Orchestration tools schedule and monitor these steps; examples in practice include pipeline frameworks that let you express dependencies and retries. A concrete example is a weekly job that ingests the previous week’s events, updates features, trains a new model, runs evaluation tests, and if metrics are good, registers and deploys the model. Misconception: orchestration is just scheduling—it's also about observability, retry semantics, and reproducible runs. Takeaway: build pipelines that are observable and testable end-to-end so production behavior is predictable. Automated ML pipelines and orchestration means automated pipelines enforce reproducibility and observability from raw data to deployed models; orchestration tools provide retries, schedules, and lineage tracking.. In practical terms, orchestrating ingestion, feature computation, training, validation, and deployment. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Process Flow Automated ML pipelines
Orchestration from ingestion to deployment
Use pipelines to enforce validation, reproducibility, and automated promotion of models.

screens.title: Feature stores and data versioning
screens.narratorSegment: Feature stores and data versioning solve the classic problem of training-serving skew and allow teams to reproduce model behavior. A feature store centralizes computation and serving of features so training and online inference use the same values. For example, computing a user’s 30-day average purchase value in one place and serving it to both training pipelines and the online prediction service prevents mismatches that silently degrade accuracy. Data versioning records which raw datasets were used for a training run; this is essential for audits and for reproducing historical models. A common mistake is to rebuild features ad-hoc in different services, which leads to inconsistency and subtle bugs. In practice you should treat features as first-class artifacts: enforce contracts, document schemas, and provide APIs for retrieval. Concrete scenario: when a product catalog field is renamed, a feature store and data versioning let you map and validate the change before it impacts a live model. Takeaway: invest in feature engineering infrastructure and dataset versioning to reduce operational risk and speed up model iteration. Feature stores and data versioning means centralize feature computation and serve consistent feature values to prevent training-serving skew and enable reproducibility.. In practical terms, consistency between training and inference, and reproducible datasets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition Feature stores & data versioning
Feature engineering as infrastructure
Treat features and datasets as managed artifacts to ensure consistency and reproducibility.
Concrete example
A user average purchase value computed once and exposed for both training and online inference avoids skew and reduces duplication.
Common pitfall
Ad-hoc feature code across services causes subtle differences and production regressions.
Operational practices
  • Feature contracts and schemas
  • API-backed feature serving for online inference
  • Dataset snapshots and version tags for training runs
Key Takeaway

Manage features and datasets centrally to reduce skew and enable reproducible model development and audits.

Scenario
When a source field changes, versioned datasets and feature store contracts let you detect the impact before deploying a new model.
Checklist
Define schemas, snapshot datasets per run, and expose features via stable APIs for online inference.

screens.title: Monitoring, drift detection, and retraining strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Monitoring is the mechanism that turns model performance from an unknown into an observable signal. Track both model quality metrics like accuracy or click-through rate and operational metrics like latency and error rate. For input stability, monitor data drift — statistical changes in feature distributions — and concept drift — changes in the relationship between inputs and targets. Concrete examples of monitoring include daily checks for distribution shifts using statistical tests and tracking business KPIs such as conversion rate for a recommender. When drift is detected, you need retraining strategies. A scheduled retraining cadence, such as weekly, ensures freshness but may waste resources when nothing has changed. Performance-triggered retraining uses alerts to start retraining only when metrics degrade. Hybrid strategies combine schedule and triggers to balance cost and responsiveness. A common misconception is relying solely on technical metrics like C P U or throughput; these say nothing about model relevance. Takeaway: monitor data and model quality, define clear alert thresholds, and choose retraining strategies that align with business cost and freshness requirements. What metric would you use to decide between scheduled and triggered retraining for your use case?

content.html:
Definition Monitoring & retraining
Detect drift and decide when to retrain
Combine statistical tests and business metrics to detect when models lose effectiveness.
What to monitor
  • Model metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, CTR
  • Data drift: statistical tests on feature distributions
  • Operational metrics: latency, errors, resource usage
Retraining options
Scheduled, triggered by performance, or hybrid approaches depending on cost and business impact.
Concrete example
Trigger retraining when click-through rate drops more than a defined percentage versus baseline, otherwise run weekly retraining to capture slow trends.
Key Takeaway

Monitoring must include business metrics as well as statistical tests; use those signals to decide retraining frequency.

Alert triggers

screens.title: Serving strategies and scalability considerations
screens.narratorSegment: Serving models requires choices about containerization, orchestration, and resource management. A typical approach is to package a prediction service in a container and run it on an orchestrator like Kubernetes for consistent scaling and observability. Serverless functions can be cost-effective for low-traffic endpoints but introduce cold start latency and may limit model size or runtime dependencies. For high-throughput online services, autoscaling groups or horizontal pod autoscaling provide predictable capacity. Use canary or shadow deployments to test new model versions against production traffic without full promotion. Concrete example: deploy a Flask or FastAPI service in a container behind a load balancer, and use horizontal scaling based on request latency and C P U. A common pitfall is failing to test model cold starts or memory usage; models with large memory footprints can cause out-of-memory errors under scale. Key operational controls include resource requests/limits, health checks, and graceful shutdown to avoid dropped in-flight requests during rollouts. Takeaway: align serving technology with traffic patterns and make scaling and rollout strategies explicit in your architecture. screens.title: Designing an MLOps pipeline for a recommender
screens.narratorSegment: This activity guides you to design a practical MLOps pipeline for a product recommender. Start by listing data sources: web logs for browsing events, a transactions table for purchases, and the product catalog for metadata. Stage one is data ingestion and ETL: extract events and transform them into stable schemas, using batch or streaming tools as appropriate. Next, materialize core features in a feature store so both training and online inference share the same values. Training occurs in a reproducible environment where experiments log metrics to a tracking service; compare candidates against a holdout and existing production model via a model registry. If the candidate passes quality gates, deploy it as an online inference endpoint for product pages, and use canary traffic to validate live behavior. Monitoring must include CTR, conversion, data drift, and endpoint latency. Retraining can be scheduled weekly but also triggered if monitoring detects a significant metric drop. A common mistake is forgetting to version data and features, which makes debugging failures difficult. Takeaway: the pipeline should be end-to-end observable, testable, and designed to promote models safely from experiment to production.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will orient around the practical work of integrating machine learning into real production systems. You will learn why ML changes architecture decisions, which deployment patterns solve different latency and coupling needs, and how MLOps practices keep models healthy over time. Think of an ML model not as a single binary but as a living element: it depends on data pipelines, feature consistency, a model registry, deployment endpoints, and monitoring. For example, an online recommendation call must guarantee low latency and consistent feature values, while a batch scoring job can trade latency for throughput. A common misconception is treating a model like static code. Instead, plan for retraining, versioning, and drift detection from day one. By the end of this chapter you will be able to map a business need — like fraud detection or personalized recommendations — to a concrete pattern, choose serving and monitoring strategies, and sketch an MLOps pipeline that supports continuous delivery. Consider a weekly retraining schedule for a recommendation engine: the pipeline must ingest new events, update features, validate a new model, and then promote it to production safely. What would you monitor first in that flow?

In this segment we'll set clear goals for what you'll be able to do after working through the lesson. First, you will identify core challenges when integrating ML into existing software, such as the need for continuous data pipelines and the probabilistic nature of models. Second, you'll recognize the main deployment patterns—online, batch, embedded, and remote—and be able to choose the right one based on latency, throughput, and coupling constraints. Third, you'll explain MLOps practices that bring automation, reproducibility, and monitoring to the model lifecycle, including model registries and CI/CD for ML artifacts. Finally, you'll evaluate data infrastructure components like feature stores and data versioning systems so models get consistent inputs in training and production. Each objective includes a short competency measure: sketch a pipeline, pick a serving pattern for a scenario, and propose monitoring and retraining triggers. These skills matter because ML systems require both architectural choices and operational discipline to avoid silent failures or performance decay in production.

This continuation focuses on operational and evaluative skills. You will learn to implement monitoring and alerting that track both model quality and input data distributions. For instance, set alerts for sudden shifts in input feature distributions or a drop in click-through rate for a recommender. You will also practice model versioning and registry usage so teams can test, compare, and promote model artifacts safely. Another objective is to select appropriate retraining strategies: scheduled retraining, performance-triggered retraining, or hybrid approaches. Each approach has trade-offs between stability and freshness. Lastly, you will assess security and governance considerations: protect training data, control access to prediction endpoints, and respect privacy constraints. Together these objectives prepare you to not only deploy models, but also keep them accurate, auditable, and compliant in production environments. Learning Objectives (Part 2) means monitoring, versioning, retraining triggers, and governance are integral skills to keep ml systems trustworthy and maintainable.. In practical terms, operational practices and evaluation criteria. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Machine learning components differ from traditional software in important ways. First, models are probabilistic: they produce predictions based on learned patterns and therefore have uncertainty. That means behavior can change when input data shifts, so you must plan for continuous evaluation. Second, models depend on data pipelines and feature computation; inconsistent feature values between training and serving cause prediction errors known as training/serving skew. Third, the development lifecycle is iterative and multi-disciplinary: data scientists experiment, ML engineers operationalize, and software engineers integrate the service. Architecturally this leads to distinct responsibilities—feature stores to centralize feature computation, model registries to manage artifacts, and deployment services to isolate inference. A concrete example is a product recommender: it needs live user features for online inference and a retraining loop to refresh weights weekly. A common misconception is to treat a model like any library you can version and forget; instead, treat it as a product that requires monitoring, governance, and scheduled updates. Takeaway: plan pipelines, enforce feature consistency, and make retraining part of the architecture. What aspect of your current application would change if a model’s predictions could drift over time?

Selecting a deployment pattern is a core architectural decision. Online inference provides low-latency predictions by exposing a model via a real-time endpoint; it is suitable for fraud detection or personalized recommendations where each request needs a decision in milliseconds. Batch inference processes large datasets at scheduled intervals and favors throughput over per-request latency, for example producing daily churn scores for marketing. Embedded models are included directly in application binaries or mobile apps; they reduce network overhead and latency but increase deployment coupling and complicate updates. Remote models are isolated in dedicated prediction services; they offer better scalability and independent lifecycle management but introduce network latency. As a concrete scenario, consider fraud scoring during checkout: online inference is typically preferred because decisions must be immediate. A common misconception is to default to embedded models for speed; however, embedded models can become stale and make rolling updates cumbersome. When choosing a pattern, weigh latency requirements, update cadence, operational complexity, and security boundaries. Which pattern would you choose if your top priority is independent scaling and version control? Deployment patterns: online, batch, embedded, remote means match pattern to requirements: online for low latency, batch for throughput, embedded for tight latency but high coupling, remote for isolation and independent scaling.. In practical terms, trade-offs across latency, coupling, and scalability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

MLOps is the operational practice that stitches together experimentation and production delivery for ML models. At its core are automation, reproducibility, and testable deployments. Start with versioning: track code, configuration, data, and model artifacts so you can reproduce results and audit changes. Model registries store artifacts, metadata, and stage transitions — for example staging to production — enabling safe promotion and rollback. CI/CD pipelines for ML should validate not only code but also data integrity and model quality gates; automated tests can include unit tests, data schema checks, and model evaluation against a holdout set. A concrete example is a pipeline that runs on new data: first it validates data schemas, then trains a candidate model, logs metrics to a tracking system, compares performance with production, and if it passes quality gates, registers and deploys the model. A common mistake is to rely on manual promotion; automation reduces human error and ensures repeatability. Takeaway: make reproducibility and automated quality checks the backbone of your ML delivery. How would you implement a safety gate that prevents a worse model from being deployed?

An automated ML pipeline strings together the stages that move raw events to a deployed model and returning value. The pipeline typically starts with data ingestion and validation: verify schemas and completeness so downstream models are not fed corrupt inputs. Next, compute and materialize features, often in a feature store that can serve both training and online requests. Then execute training and hyperparameter tuning, followed by validation against holdout datasets and business-specific quality gates. If the candidate passes gates, register the model and trigger a deployment step—this may be a canary rollout or a full promotion to production. Orchestration tools schedule and monitor these steps; examples in practice include pipeline frameworks that let you express dependencies and retries. A concrete example is a weekly job that ingests the previous week’s events, updates features, trains a new model, runs evaluation tests, and if metrics are good, registers and deploys the model. Misconception: orchestration is just scheduling—it's also about observability, retry semantics, and reproducible runs. Takeaway: build pipelines that are observable and testable end-to-end so production behavior is predictable. Automated ML pipelines and orchestration means automated pipelines enforce reproducibility and observability from raw data to deployed models; orchestration tools provide retries, schedules, and lineage tracking.. In practical terms, orchestrating ingestion, feature computation, training, validation, and deployment. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Feature stores and data versioning solve the classic problem of training-serving skew and allow teams to reproduce model behavior. A feature store centralizes computation and serving of features so training and online inference use the same values. For example, computing a user’s 30-day average purchase value in one place and serving it to both training pipelines and the online prediction service prevents mismatches that silently degrade accuracy. Data versioning records which raw datasets were used for a training run; this is essential for audits and for reproducing historical models. A common mistake is to rebuild features ad-hoc in different services, which leads to inconsistency and subtle bugs. In practice you should treat features as first-class artifacts: enforce contracts, document schemas, and provide APIs for retrieval. Concrete scenario: when a product catalog field is renamed, a feature store and data versioning let you map and validate the change before it impacts a live model. Takeaway: invest in feature engineering infrastructure and dataset versioning to reduce operational risk and speed up model iteration. Monitoring is the mechanism that turns model performance from an unknown into an observable signal. Track both model quality metrics like accuracy or click-through rate and operational metrics like latency and error rate. For input stability, monitor data drift — statistical changes in feature distributions — and concept drift — changes in the relationship between inputs and targets. Concrete examples of monitoring include daily checks for distribution shifts using statistical tests and tracking business KPIs such as conversion rate for a recommender. When drift is detected, you need retraining strategies. A scheduled retraining cadence, such as weekly, ensures freshness but may waste resources when nothing has changed. Performance-triggered retraining uses alerts to start retraining only when metrics degrade. Hybrid strategies combine schedule and triggers to balance cost and responsiveness. A common misconception is relying solely on technical metrics like C P U or throughput; these say nothing about model relevance. Takeaway: monitor data and model quality, define clear alert thresholds, and choose retraining strategies that align with business cost and freshness requirements.
